title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
dek: Cash use is dwindling, yet the dollar in circulation is at a record high. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: that money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, at the cost of enabling global money launderers.
why: This episode breaks down money laundering into watches, tractors, casino chips, and VAT loopholes—not just bank wires—and explains why central banks are reluctant to retire the $100 bill.
who: Bank compliance officers, cross-border payment and monetary policy professionals, and anyone curious why killing the $100 bill is so hard.
skip: The first about 4 minutes are a live event ad and small talk; skip to 5:09 to start listening.

points.h: Money laundering scale hasn't changed in 30 years
points.body: The most commonly cited estimate for money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP annually—roughly $2 trillion to $5 trillion on today's ~$100 trillion GDP. That figure traces back to a rough guess by former IMF chief Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and no one has come up with a better answer since. Oliver warns that what should worry us more is that the ratio hasn't budged in three decades: decades of anti-money laundering efforts haven't shrunk the criminal economy; they've barely kept it from growing faster than the overall economy.

points.h: Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML with near-zero effect
points.body: Bank complaints about KYC costs aren't just whining. The 1970 Bank Secrecy Act in the U.S. and the FATF's global push since 1989 forced banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs around $200 billion a year—enough to end world hunger and provide clean water to everyone. But the system churns out massive numbers of suspicious activity reports, and launderers still stay ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is costly, has weak feedback, and almost no one is held accountable for results.

Cash smuggling makes bank-based laundering look small, but the bigger chunk never touches money: value is hidden in goods. Mexico sees about $25 billion in cash flow in each year, while U.S. exports of John Deere and Caterpillar equipment become the goods drug cartels get in return; European luxury goods flow to China, and from China drugs and merchandise are imported back, with the triangle settled through misinvoicing. Global Financial Integrity estimates trade-based laundering at around $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch worn through customs is far easier than hauling a million in cash.

points.h: The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets drug supply
points.body: China caps each person's annual foreign exchange at $50,000, yet wealthy Chinese have plenty of overseas spending needs. The Vancouver model matches that demand with drug cartels' supply of U.S. dollars: cash bags are handed to Chinese gamblers outside Canadian casinos, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers owe a debt. That debt is offset by yuan transactions on the Chinese side and by subsequent drug sales. Viewed alone, the gambling looks like a loss; across the whole chain, it's a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates drug money and moves Chinese capital out. The model has since gone global, with luxury goods, everyday items, and drugs all serving as value carriers.

points.h: VAT loophole lets the same goods repeatedly extract 20%
points.body: The EU's zero-rated cross-border transactions were meant to avoid tax authorities chasing each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland avoid VAT, then a 20% markup is added when sold to a related shell company; that shell exports the goods back to Ireland and claims a refund from the UK tax authority for the 20% that was never paid. Round and round, hence the name carousel fraud. The UK largely suppressed it with multi-agency crackdowns, but fraudsters moved to the continent, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, stretching from Lithuania to Portugal. Criminal organizations face no cap on competition: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

points.h: Nobody uses cash, yet central banks print record amounts
points.body: In the digital payment era, cash transactions are only about 9% of the total in the UK and 13% in the US, so paper currency supply should logically shrink. Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey articulated the banknote paradox in 2009, and since then the phenomenon has intensified: UK notes in circulation have doubled in value, and the US is close to $2.5 trillion. Central banks' explanation of 'store of value' doesn't hold—surveys show the average American adult has only a few hundred dollars on hand, while per capita currency in circulation exceeds $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. notes are abroad, but that just pushes the question across borders: no one knows who actually holds those notes.

points.h: The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
points.body: Seigniorage isn't simply profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents to produce, but it isn't 'sold' to you—you can redeem it for goods at face value at any time, so public cash holdings are essentially an interest-free loan. With nearly $2.5 trillion in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funds equal to about 6% of its debt; federal interest payments are already about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion had to pay interest, it would add another percentage point. That's why central banks don't want to hear talk of abolishing the bill.

points.h: AML incentives are backwards: more reports, less crime prosecuted
points.body: Suspicious activity reports were meant to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to file reports, law enforcement lacks resources to read them, and most reports go into a black hole. Banks can be fined billions for missing a report, but get no reward for doing it right. Side effects include debanking—large numbers of suspected people, many of them Muslim, get cut off from financial institutions. The guests' solution isn't more compliance officers but generating fewer reports, actually reading them, and genuinely prosecuting financial criminals—raising the cost of laundering rather than drowning everyone in paperwork.

quotes.text: But the most widely used estimate is that We're talking about between 2% and 5% of global GDP. And since global GDP is approximately $ 100 trillion, that means between $ 2 and $ 5 trillion being laundered globally.

Cash is a hugely significant tool for moving illicit wealth around the world. And even that is dwarfed by what we refer to as trade-based money laundering. It is essentially a way of moving value around the world, not in the form of money at all, but in the form of stuff.

So there is very little demand for cash from society. So you would expect, therefore, the supply of cash to be collapsing. And yet at the same time that the demand is very low, For some reason, supply is very, very high and getting higher all the time, consistently, almost everywhere.

if you take a $ 100 bill out the bank, you're not actually buying that $ 100 bill because you can sell it back at any time for the same amount that you bought it for. So actually, it's an interest-free loan to the government is what it really is.
if the US stops producing its $ 100 bill, and I wish it would, I don't think that there is anyone really, who would be inconvenienced by the lack of $ 100 bills except the bad guys.

Criminals have always liked to stack different techniques on top of each other. And so, yeah, cash remains the most useful criminal tool at a street level. But it's bulky, it's not secure. It's kind of annoying and smelly. It's annoying to count and so on. So if you can get away from using that as quickly as possible in order to move it around the world, that's where crypto comes in and is super useful.

Instead, we have a system that piles a huge amount of paperwork on financial institutions and a huge amount of expense and occasionally fines them for their trouble, but doesn't really do anything to stop financial crime. And that's kind of, as we say in Britain, ass backwards.
